anchor_text: O that this too too solid flesh would melt
summary: The First Folio (1623) reads 'solid'; the Second Quarto (1604–05) reads 'sallied' (an old form of 'sullied,' meaning stained or defiled). Some editors prefer 'sullied' because it initiates the play's imagery of corruption and contamination, whereas 'solid' fits the wish to dissolve into water. The debate remains open among modern editors.
detail: If 'sullied,' Hamlet's disgust is directed inward — his flesh is already tainted by his mother's sin. If 'solid,' the longing is Platonic: the heavy material body is the prison the soul wants to escape. The Oxford Shakespeare (1987) and Arden 3 (2006) both present the choice as genuinely contested. See also the First Quarto's 'sallied,' which supports the 'sullied' camp orthographically.

summary: In Elizabethan canon law (derived from Leviticus), marriage to a deceased brother's wife was classified as incest. summary: This is one of the most debated cruxes in all of Shakespeare. The First Quarto (Q1, 1603) omits the passage; the Second Quarto (Q2, 1604–5) prints 'eale'; the First Folio (F1, 1623) prints 'evil.' No reading is fully satisfying. 'Dram of eale' has been emended to 'dram of evil,' 'dram of ill,' 'dram of base,' and more. The basic sense in context is clear — a tiny quantity of something bad corrupts the whole — but the exact word Shakespeare wrote remains unknown.
detail: Q2's 'eale' is almost certainly a compositor's misreading of a secretary-hand manuscript; the most widely accepted emendation is 'evil' (F1's reading), which fits the sense: 'a dram of evil doth all the noble substance often dout [i.e., extinguish] / To his own scandal.' The verb 'doubt' in the next line (Q2) may itself be a misprint of 'dout' (extinguish a candle), but the Folio reads 'oft doubt.' Jenkins (Arden 2) and Thompson & Taylor (Arden 3) both discuss the crux at length without reaching firm consensus.

summary: The Ghost describes a place of cleansing punishment between death and Heaven — the Catholic doctrine of Purgatory, where souls atone for sins 'not yet burnt and purged away.' The scene's horror depends on this ambiguity.

anchor_text: O, what a rogue and peasant slave am I!
summary: The opening of Hamlet's great self-excoriation soliloquy. "Rogue" = a vagrant or worthless fellow (archaic); "peasant slave" stresses social abasement — the opposite of a prince. Hamlet condemns himself by contrast with the Player who wept real tears for Hecuba, a fictional character, while Hamlet does nothing for his murdered father.

summary: Hecuba was the queen of Troy, wife of Priam, who watched her husband and children slaughtered during the city's fall. In Greek tradition she became the archetype of catastrophic grief. Hamlet's point: the Player weeps for a legendary queen he has no connection to, yet Hamlet — with a real murdered father — cannot act. The rhetorical antimetabole ("Hecuba to him / he to Hecuba") sharpens the paradox.

summary: "John-a-dreams" was a proverbial phrase for a dreamy, inactive person — someone who drifts through life asleep to what matters. "Unpregnant" = not full of, not quickened or stirred by (his cause for revenge). Hamlet accuses himself of being passive and empty when he should be burning to act.

anchor_text: I am pigeon-liver'd, and lack gall
summary: In Elizabethan physiology, the liver was the seat of courage and passion, and bile ("gall") produced fierceness. Pigeons were believed to have no gall bladder and therefore no bitterness — they would bear any injury meekly. Hamlet calls himself cowardly by comparing himself to a pigeon: too gentle and passive to make oppression feel bitter enough to fight back against.

summary: Protestant theology — especially as understood by Elizabethan audiences — taught that the devil could masquerade as a dead person's spirit in order to tempt the living into sin. This is why he needs the play to independently confirm Claudius's guilt.

summary: In Elizabethan cant, 'nunnery' was slang for a brothel — a usage documented in Thomas Dekker and other contemporary writers. anchor_text: My words fly up, my thoughts remain below

The couplet is also a stichoymythic epigram — a self-contained two-line conclusion that flips the scene's premise. Claudius has been trying to pray (words going up) but we know his heart is not in it (thoughts remaining earthbound). In Protestant theology, prayer that is only words, without genuine contrition, is worthless.

summary: The rood is the cross (Old English 'rod'). 'By the rood' is a common Elizabethan mild oath, swearing by Christ's crucifix. It marks Hamlet's oath as genuine but also edged with irony — he is about to define his mother in the most brutal terms.

summary: A ducat was a gold coin used across Europe; the phrase means 'I'll bet a ducat he's dead' — a gambler's wager shouted at the moment of the thrust. Hamlet is so certain the hidden man is mortally struck that he bets on it. The casual, sporting tone makes the killing more chilling.

summary: Front = brow or forehead (archaic). Jove (Jupiter/Zeus) was the king of the gods, proverbially depicted with a commanding, massive brow. The phrase pictures the dead king's forehead as bearing the authority and majesty of the ruler of Olympus — kingly by divine nature.

anchor_text: A station like the herald Mercury
summary: Station = posture, stance (archaic). Mercury (Hermes in Greek myth) was the gods' swift messenger, always depicted poised mid-step on a hilltop — the ideal of graceful readiness. summary: Hamlet compares Claudius to a blighted ear of grain — a mildewed stalk that spreads disease to a healthy one. anchor_text: The hey-day in the blood is tame

summary: The Vice was the central comic villain of medieval English morality plays — a boisterous, dagger-waving clown who represented evil while making the audience laugh. anchor_text:
a certain

summary: A double pun: a 'convocation' is a formal assembly (like a parliament or church synod), and 'politic' means shrewd, statesman-like. Shakespeare is riffing on the Diet of Worms — a famous Imperial assembly held in the German city of Worms in 1521 where Martin Luther was condemned. The joke layers the political meeting on top of the literal grave-worms eating Polonius's body.
detail: The Diet of Worms (1521) was one of the most famous political assemblies in recent European memory: the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V presided, and Luther refused to recant his Reformation doctrines. 'Diet' = an assembly of estates (German 'Reichstag'); 'Worms' = the city on the Rhine. Shakespeare collapses this into a mordant joke: the worms gnawing at Polonius are holding their own imperial 'diet' (meal and assembly at once), and they are 'politic' — politically savvy, like courtiers. A 1601 London audience would have caught the Diet of Worms reference immediately.

summary: This is one of the play's most compressed paradoxes. Hamlet appears to argue that true greatness does NOT require a major grievance — that a great man will fight over nothing ('a straw') if his honor demands it. But the logic is double-edged: Hamlet himself has the biggest possible cause (a murdered father, a corrupted kingdom) and still doesn't act, while Fortinbras risks thousands of lives over dirt. The speech simultaneously admires and quietly questions the honor code it seems to endorse.

anchor_text: My thoughts be bloody, or be nothing worth!
summary: The soliloquy ends with a brisk rhyming couplet (worth / forth), a conventional signal in Elizabethan drama that a speech is closing. The irony the audience carries out of the scene is that Hamlet immediately sails to England rather than back to Elsinore — the bloody thoughts remain thoughts.

anchor_text:
By his cockle bat and' staff

In Renaissance love-poetry, a pilgrim journeying to his saint became a standard image for a lover seeking his beloved — giving Ophelia's song a double meaning.

summary: The Elizabethan folk belief was that the first person of the opposite sex you saw on the morning of February 14 became your valentine — your lover for the year. Ophelia's song exploits this custom: a girl goes to her lover's window at dawn to be his valentine, but the song quickly turns into a seduction-and-abandonment story (he lets her in, and she 'never departed more' as a maid). The valentine frame makes the betrayal sharper.

Shakespeare's audience knew this doctrine well; Claudius's invoking it is deeply ironic, since he himself committed the ultimate treason by murdering a king.

summary: Rue (the plant) carried the meanings of repentance, sorrow, and pity — the word 'rue' also means to regret in English, which Shakespeare exploits. anchor_text: as a woodcock to my own springe, Osric
summary: A woodcock was the classic proverbially stupid bird — easy to trap because it walks straight into a snare ('springe'). A springe is a simple wire noose set in a path. Laertes acknowledges poetic justice: he set the lethal trap for Hamlet and has stumbled into it himself.

sources.name: OED s.v. springe
sources.citation: OED s.v. springe n.: 'a snare for catching birds or small game, consisting of a noose attached to a bent branch.'

sources.name: Tilley, Dictionary of Proverbs
sources.citation: Tilley, M. P. (1950). A Dictionary of Proverbs in England. University of Michigan Press. W740: 'The woodcock near the gin (snare)' — proverbial for easy entrapment.

sources.name: Jenkins (Arden 2 Hamlet, 1982)

summary: A 'sergeant' in Elizabethan law was a sheriff's officer whose job was to serve legal warrants and physically arrest people. 'Fell' = fierce, cruel. 'Strict in his arrest' = makes his seizure without exception. Hamlet personifies Death as an implacable bailiff who will not be argued with — coming for him right now, mid-sentence, before he can tell his full story.

anchor_text: I am more an antique Roman than a Dane
summary: Horatio invokes the Roman Stoic ideal of voluntary death: Roman heroes such as Cato the Younger and Brutus chose suicide rather than survive in dishonor or outlive their cause. A 'Dane' by contrast implies survival in a world of pragmatic compromise. Reaching for the poisoned cup, Horatio says he would rather die the Roman way than live on without Hamlet.

sources.name: Plutarch (North 1579), Cato the Younger
sources.citation: Plutarch, Lives, 'Cato the Younger' §70 (trans. North 1579): Cato's suicide at Utica as the archetypal honorable Roman death.

sources.name: Jenkins (Arden 2 Hamlet, 1982)
sources.citation: Jenkins, Harold, ed. (1982). Hamlet, Arden 2. Methuen. p. 409 n. 3827.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3827

Plutarch's Life of Cato the Younger is real; Cato's suicide at Utica is in the text (sections 66-70 area). North's 1579 translation is confirmed. Jenkins Arden 2 real. Roman Stoic suicide parallel is standard scholarship.
Roman Stoic voluntary death (Cato, Brutus) as referent is the mainstream scholarly reading; Plutarch parallel is conventional; contrast with Danish pragmatic survival is defensible.

anchor_text: The potent poison quite o'er-crows my spirit
summary: 'O'er-crows' means to crow over in triumph, as a victorious cock crows over a defeated rival. The poison is beating down Hamlet's spirit the way a stronger bird beats a weaker one — crowing its victory. It is also a pun on 'overcomes.'

summary: 'Rest' carries two senses simultaneously: (1) the remainder, what is left over — there are no more words; (2) rest as in peace, stillness, cessation. The dying Hamlet, who has talked throughout the play, ends in wordlessness. The ambiguity is thematically essential: silence as the only honest answer to death.

summary: Horatio's farewell draws on the Christian belief in angels escorting the righteous dead to heaven. The image echoes Luke 16:22 in the Geneva Bible (the angels carry Lazarus to Abraham's bosom) and the tradition of the 'requiem' — a prayer for the soul's rest. Calling Hamlet a 'sweet prince' at the moment of valediction is a formal funeral act.

summary: 'Quarry' is the heap of slain game at the end of a hunt — all the bodies piled together. 'Cries on havoc' means proclaims (or calls out) 'havoc,' the military signal to begin unrestricted killing and plunder. Fortinbras arrives and sees four royal corpses: the scene looks like the aftermath of a military massacre, not a fencing match.

anchor_text: I have some rights of memory in this kingdom
summary: 'Rights of memory' = rights that are remembered, kept on record — old or dormant legal claims. Fortinbras's father was defeated and killed by Hamlet's father, forfeiting his lands; Fortinbras's uncle later made peace with Denmark. Now with the Danish royal line extinct, Fortinbras revives those old territorial claims. His arrival and succession end the play's political vacuum.

anchor_text: The soldiers' music and the rites of war
summary: Fortinbras orders Hamlet carried out with full military honors — a drum march and cannon volley — because Hamlet was a prince who would likely have been a great king. The play ends not with a prayer or a sermon but with martial noise: a soldier's funeral that transforms the Danish court's carnage into something more like a heroic death on the battlefield.
